- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or shift downward by 2–5%.
- If sentiment is positive (≥0.67) and prices are trending upward, model often over-optimistically forecasts continuation; cap upward momentum at 1–2% above recent peak.
- When true outcome shows sharp downward spike (e.g., >10% drop from prior day), model frequently fails to adjust; add a 3–5 day lagged correction buffer.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below forecast), reduce forecast slope by 10–20%.
- In sentiment-neutral or mixed periods, model often overfits recent history; apply smoothing filter or use 30-day moving average as baseline.
- If forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows strong upward momentum, model underestimates breakout; increase forecast by 3–5% for next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment turns negative after a spike, model often overshoots and fails to correct; apply “sentiment decay” rule: reduce forecast by 1–2% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
